title: Makahiya: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Makahiya in Rice Fields: Identification and Control
metaDescription: Makahiya is a thorny, touch sensitive weed of rainfed palay. Learn to spot it, handle its spines safely, and keep it from seeding in your field.
excerpt: Makahiya is the low, thorny shrub whose leaves fold shut the moment you touch them. It looks harmless, but in the bukid it is a weed of rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it among the palay, handle its spines safely, and control it before it seeds.

heroImage.alt: Sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica), a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields

blocks.text:
Makahiya is the sensitive plant, Mimosa pudica, from the Mimosaceae family. Farmers also know it as Bain bain, hibi hibi, huya huya, kipi kipi and makahiyang babae. That last name sets it apart from its bigger, spinier cousin, the giant sensitive plant. Since it is a broadleaf weed, it is not a grass or a sedge.

You will see it in rainfed lowland rice fields, where the soil is not always flooded. As a perennial, one plant can live on for more than one season. Seed is how it spreads. Each plant makes many flat, slightly curved pods, and the seeds fall around it. Its stems branch low or trail along the ground, so a few plants can soon form a spiny mat.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about makahiya
rows: Bain bain, hibi hibi, huya huya, kipi kipi, makahiya, makahiyang babae

blocks.text: The easiest test is to touch it, because the leaves fold up right away. Look for a low, branched shrub that trails or stands upright, with reddish brown stems carrying scattered spines. Each leaf stalk ends in a few leaflet branches spread like fingers, each with many narrow leaflets. Like other broadleaf weeds, its leaflets have netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. The flowers are pink to purple, and the pods are flat, slightly curved and many.

items: Leaves that fold shut within seconds when you touch or brush them.
Low, branched stems that trail along the ground or stand upright.
Reddish brown stems with scattered spines that prick bare hands.
Leaflet branches spread like fingers at the tip of each leaf stalk.
Pink to purple flowers, followed by many flat, slightly curved pods.
Look alike tip: the giant sensitive plant is bigger, much spinier, with 4 to 8 pairs of leaf branches.

blocks.text:
This weed may look small and harmless, but it takes water, fertilizer and space from your palay. Its trailing, branched stems spread low and form a mat between the rice hills. In rainfed fields, where water can run short, every bit of moisture counts.

The spines cause trouble too. They prick the hands and legs of farmers who weed, transplant or harvest near it, so people tend to skip those patches. As a result, the weed grows unchecked. Because it is a perennial, it can stay in the field and on the bunds season after season. Each plant also makes many pods that fill the soil with seed.

items: Wear gloves when you pull it, because the stems carry spines that prick and scratch bare hands.
Pull or dig out plants with their roots before the pink flowers turn into pods, so no new seed drops.
Clear it from bunds and field edges too, since this perennial survives there between croppings and spreads seed back into the paddy.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold makahiya down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. You can also put the weeding days on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), so the team knows when to go in.

items.q: What is makahiya called in other Philippine languages?
items.a: Farmers also call it Bain bain, hibi hibi, huya huya, kipi kipi or makahiyang babae. Its English name is sensitive plant, and its scientific name is Mimosa pudica. Be careful with kipi kipi, since that name is also used for the giant sensitive plant. To be sure, look for a low plant with fewer spines and leaflets spread like fingers.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Wear gloves, then pull or dig out young plants with their roots before they flower. Clear the bunds and field edges too, since this perennial survives there. Keep water in the field where you can. If you need a herbicide, choose one for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why do its leaves close when touched?
items.a: Small swollen joints sit at the base of each leaflet and leaf stalk. When you touch the plant, cells in these joints quickly lose water, so the leaflets fold and droop. After a few minutes, they open again. This does not weaken the weed at all, so touching it will not help you control it.
